item.title: Exploring student and teacher perspectives on critical thinking with generative AI: early insights from the EduPartnerAI platform
item.description:
Smart Learning Environments
Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has raised important questions about its implications for students’ analytical reasoning and independent judgment. ChatGPT, a generative AI model capable of producing human-like responses, is widely used in academic contexts, yet its educational value requires careful evaluation. This paper presents and evaluates EduPartnerAI, a platform that integrates ChatGPT into student assignments and is designed to encourage critical engagement with AI-generated content. The platform records student-AI interactions, requires students to reflect on ChatGPT’s outputs, and provides teachers with tools to review observable indicators of student reasoning and AI response quality. An exploratory study involving 61 undergraduate students was conducted, relying on student reflection questionnaires, a usability survey, teacher evaluations, and an analysis of recorded interactions. Students generally perceived ChatGPT as a useful learning tool that provided clear explanations and practical examples, although some recognized that its responses could be overly general or incomplete. The teacher observed that students asked relevant questions and effectively incorporated AI-generated content into their assignments but experienced some difficulties with error detection, independent judgment, and critical evaluation. The teacher also judged ChatGPT’s outputs to be largely relevant, clear, and accurate, with few instances of bias or misleading information. Overall, the findings provide preliminary insights into student and teacher perspectives and observable patterns of engagement, highlighting both the educational potential of generative AI and the need for appropriate instructional scaffolding.

item.title: Anxiety as fuel? FoMO-AI and employee creativity through creative process engagement: the moderating roles of growth mindset and critical thinking
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Using the transactional theory of stress and coping (TTSC) as an overarching stressor–response framework, compensatory control theory (CCT) to explain compensatory engagement, and conservation of resources (COR) theory to explain resource-based boundary conditions, this study examines whether fear of missing out on artificial intelligence (FoMO-AI) is associated with self-reported employee creativity through creative process engagement (CPE) and whether growth mindset and critical thinking condition this indirect association. A three-wave, time-lagged survey was conducted with 320 employees recruited through the Credamo platform in China. The hypothesized model, which did not include a direct FoMO-AI-to-creativity path, was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap samples. A separately estimated direct-path sensitivity model and necessary condition analysis (NCA) provided complementary assessments. In the hypothesized model, FoMO-AI was positively associated with CPE (β = 0.461, p < 0.001), CPE was positively associated with creativity (β = 0.520, p < 0.001), and the hypothesized indirect effect was 0.240 ( p < 0.001). The FoMO-AI–CPE association was stronger at higher levels of growth mindset (β = 0.505, p < 0.001), and the CPE–creativity association was stronger at higher levels of critical thinking (β = 0.190, p = 0.002). The results supported a first-stage moderated mediation pattern and conditionally supported a second-stage moderated mediation pattern, which was significant at the mean and high levels of growth mindset but not at the low level. In the separately estimated direct-path sensitivity model, the added FoMO-AI-to-creativity path (β = 0.417, p < 0.001) and the corresponding indirect effect through CPE (β = 0.197, p < 0.001) were significant, whereas the critical-thinking interaction was nonsignificant (β = 0.042, p = 0.321). Estimates from the sensitivity model were not used to evaluate the hypotheses. NCA identified moderate, sample-bound necessity effects for CPE (CR-FDH: d = 0.173, p < 0.001) and critical thinking (CR-FDH: d = 0.109, p = 0.034), whereas the effect for growth mindset was nonsignificant. These necessity results do not imply sufficiency or causality. The single-country, non-probability platform sample, panel attrition, reliance on self-reports, and lack of direct measures of stress appraisal and coping limit causal, population-level, and cross-cultural generalization. The findings should therefore be interpreted as sample-bound associations among the retained Chinese employees. Future research should use organizational, probability-based, and cross-national samples, collect supervisor-rated or behavioral creativity outcomes, and examine appraisal and coping processes directly. This study identifies an indirect association between FoMO-AI and self-reported creativity through CPE and clarifies stage-specific, resource-based boundary conditions. The separately estimated direct-path sensitivity model reveals a residual FoMO-AI–creativity association and indicates that the critical-thinking result is model-dependent, thereby qualifying a uniformly beneficial interpretation of FoMO-AI.

item.title: CogChat: Knowledge Graph-Augmented Conversational AI with Heterogeneous Graph Transformer for Cognitive Grounding in Design Generation
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
LLM-based chat systems have become valuable tools for design practice, enabling rapid ideation and flexible task support. Yet these systems process designer utterances as generic sequences, maintaining context through recency rather than through any model of how the speaker organizes knowledge. In design conversation, this gap compounds as relational context decays between turns, identical words go unresolved across designers, and the conversation loops or restarts rather than deepens. We present CogChat, a real-time chat framework that grounds conversational AI in a personal heterogeneous knowledge graph constructed from each designer’s input. The system extracts typed entities and relations into a heterogeneous graph, then applies a HGT (Heterogeneous Graph Transformer) to select structurally relevant nodes for response generation and to generate both intentional and exploratory probing questions. Technical evaluation shows that HGT-based entity selection outperforms both ungrounded LLM interaction and naïve KG augmentation, which introduces noise that degrades response quality. A within-subjects study with nine professional designers indicates that grounding conversation in a relationally structured, designer-specific semantic context improves context retention, personalized intent interpretation, and conversational depth while reducing cognitive load. These findings suggest that structuring a designer’s expressed concepts and relations as a dynamic knowledge graph can preserve relational context that fades across turns, pointing toward a graph-grounded approach to long-term context management in LLM-based interaction.

item.title: ImageDirector: Expressing Spatial Intent via 3D Direct Manipulation for Generative Image Editing
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Generative image editing through text prompting suffers from two fundamental limitations: text is imprecise for specifying spatial changes, and iterative edits often introduce unwanted visual drift. In contrast, people naturally approach image editing with a compositor’s intuition: manipulating individual objects while expecting the rest of the scene to remain intact. We present ImageDirector, a generative image editing system that supports this intuition by enabling users to manipulate objects in a 2D generated image as if they exist in 3D space. Given a generated image, our system segments a selected object, turns it into a manipulable high-fidelity 3D proxy via image-to-3D lifting, and lets users reposition, rotate, and scale it through direct manipulation. The system then re-composites and harmonizes the result with background regions preserved. In a within-subjects study (N = 12), ImageDirector significantly outperformed a text-only prompting baseline in spatial accuracy and visual consistency across iterative edits; participants also reported substantially greater perceived control and expressiveness over the editing process. Finally, we discuss how this approach extends to broader content creation workflows, opening new possibilities for intuitive, precise, and controllable human-AI co-creation.

item.title: Editrail: Understanding AI Usage by Visualizing Student-AI Interaction in Code
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Programming instructors have diverse philosophies about integrating generative AI into their classes. Some encourage students to use AI, while others restrict or forbid it. Regardless of their approach, all instructors benefit from understanding how their students actually use AI while writing code [1, 14, 25, 38]. Such insight helps instructors assess whether AI use aligns with their pedagogical goals, enables timely intervention when they find unproductive usage patterns, and establishes effective policies for AI use. However, our survey with programming instructors found that many instructors lack visibility into how students use AI in their code-writing processes. To address this challenge, we introduce Editrail, an interactive system that enables instructors to track students’ AI usage, create personalized assessments, and provide timely interventions, all within the workflow of monitoring coding histories. We found that Editrail enables instructors to accurately detect AI use that conflicts with pedagogical goals and to determine when and which students require intervention.

item.title: Treellis: Exposing Editable Assembly Structures for Progressive Human-AI Co-Creation of 3D Models
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Generative AI lowers the barriers to 3D modeling but offers limited control over outcomes. We present Treellis, a human-AI co-creation tool for 3D modeling. Given a text prompt, Treellis produces a 3D object along with a user interface that reveals its component-level assembly structure and in-situ editable parameters. This enables users to inspect and iteratively refine problematic regions of the model at multiple levels of granularity using both AI-assisted operations and direct manual edits, while preserving usable substructures unaffected. Across a between-subject controlled study and a multi-session open-ended study, we found that Treellis helped users develop efficient hybrid strategies between AI and manual to create complex 3D designs. Results also show that exposing AI-generated 3D artifacts as editable assembly structures can support localized repair and reduce refinement friction in human-AI 3D co-creation.

item.title: TeachUp: Facilitating Early-Stage Teachers to Learn Instructional Strategies from Classroom Videos with Reflective Support
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Recorded videos of offline open classes provide good examples for early-stage teachers to learn instructional strategies, e.g., how to organize cooperative learning. However, learning by watching these videos is challenging, as these strategies are implicitly performed, and it lacks in-situ reflective support. In this paper, via a formative study (N=9), we design TeachUp to support the learning of instructional strategies from classroom teaching videos. TeachUp adopts an LLM-powered pipeline to detect nine instructional strategies in videos (precision = 63.4%), provides reflective questions and hints while watching, and generates customized practices with reflective feedback. A within-subjects study (N=16) shows that compared to a traditional video-playing and self-practicing baseline, early-stage teachers with TeachUp are more engaged in learning and perform better in applying learned strategies to new tasks. Interviews with four in-service teachers further generalize our findings and TeachUp’s use cases. We discuss practical implications for fostering video-based learning of instructional strategies.

item.title: Democratizing Extensive Reading by Tailoring Web Content
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Extensive reading helps foreign language learners build proficiency through large amounts of interesting, level-appropriate text. However, providing enough material matched to learners’ interests and evolving proficiency is resource-intensive and difficult to sustain. To address this challenge, we present Adapt-ER, a browser extension that leverages the web to support scalable self-selected reading by adapting pages in place to each learner’s vocabulary profile. Adapt-ER estimates lexical proficiency, tailors web content in real time, and supports lightweight profile refinement through click-based interactive learner feedback during reading. To make adaptation practical during live browsing, we compare LLM-based strategies and develop a hybrid pipeline that balances lexical difficulty control, semantic preservation, latency, and cost. In a within-subject study, Adapt-ER increased reading speed, reduced the need for dictionary and translation support during reading, and improved self-reported engagement. Our findings suggest that in-place adaptation of self-selected web text can make web reading better suited to sustained extensive reading.

item.title: Social.Wiki: A Web Held in Common
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Many of the websites people depend on have owners whose interests are not fully aligned with their users. We address the root of this problem by presenting a reimagining of the web where sites are not owned at all but are instead collaboratively produced like Wikipedia articles. We call the system Social.Wiki because it supports the co-creation of interactive social sites, such as those for microblogging, messaging, dating, gaming, ride sharing, and so on. With off-the-shelf AI tools, people with little or no programming experience can edit these sites to better reflect the needs and preferences of their communities. Social.Wiki builds on ideas from collaborative malleable software systems such as Webstrates, but is designed for public participation rather than use only within small, trusted groups. To this end, Social.Wiki includes governance to mitigate conflict. To accommodate diverse governance preferences, our model of “ plural governance ” lets people independently choose the policies that determine which edits to a site they see. Social.Wiki also implements a granular security model to protect personal data in a malleable environment. Complementing the decentralized design and governance of Social.Wiki sites, both site edits and within-site data are stored on Graffiti, a decentralized infrastructure, decoupling the ownership of underlying servers from the ownership of sites. We evaluate Social.Wiki through case studies that demonstrate the range of sociotechnical structures it supports, as well as through deployments at a hackathon and in the wild.

item.title: "What Are You Really Trying to Do?": Co-Creating Life Goals from Everyday Computer Use
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Recent advances in user modeling make it feasible to conduct open-ended inference over a person’s everyday computer use. Despite longstanding visions of systems that deeply understand our actions and the purposes they serve in our lives, existing systems only capture what a person is doing in the moment, not why they are doing it, limiting these systems to surface-level support. We introduce striving co-creation, a process for inferring broader life goals from unstructured observations of computer use. Grounded in Activity Theory and Emmons’ personal strivings framework, our system progressively constructs a hierarchical representation of a person’s activities. Strivings are, however, difficult to fully resolve from observation alone, as the same action can be driven by many different goals. Our system therefore supports an editing interface that gives people agency over how they are understood by the system, feeding their corrections back into subsequent rounds of striving induction. In a week-long field deployment (N = 14), we find that our co-creation process produces strivings that participants recognize as representative of their long-term goals and gives them greater agency than baseline methods.

item.title: PACEE: Parent-Centered AI Scaffolding for Emotion Education in Early Childhood Conversations
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Emotion education is critical for children aged 3 to 6. However, existing technologies depend substantially on direct child-AI interaction, overlooking the central role of parents in guiding early emotional development at home. To address this gap, we conducted co-design sessions with five kindergarten teachers and five parents to identify key parental challenges and opportunities for AI support in family emotion education. Based on these insights, we developed PACEE, an LLM-based assistant designed around an asymmetric triadic interaction framework: AI primarily supports parents while preserving parent-child interaction. PACEE provides parent-centered AI scaffolding that supports parents in real-time conversation through personalized guidance, post-hoc reflection through trackable feedback, and understanding children’s emotional states through modeling. We evaluated PACEE with 16 families. Results showed that PACEE increased parent-child conversational engagement and improved parents’ overall experience when guiding emotion-related conversations. Together, we contribute an asymmetric triadic interaction framework for AI-supported family education, offering design insights for AI systems that support parents while preserving parent-led parent–child interaction.

item.title: Explorable Proofs: Making Written Proofs Explorable by Grounding Them in Formal Representations
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
LLM-generated explanations can make technical content more accessible, but there is a ceiling on what they can support interactively. Because LLM outputs are static text, they cannot be executed, tinkered with, or stepped through. In this paper, we explore how grounding explanations in a formalized representation enables interactive affordances beyond what static text supports. We instantiate this idea for mathematical proof comprehension in explorable proofs, an approach that uses LLMs to translate a theorem and its written proof into Lean, a programming language for machine-checked proofs, and links the written proof with the Lean code. Readers can work through the proof at a step-level granularity, test custom examples or counterexamples, and trace the logical dependencies bridging between steps. Each worked-out step is produced by executing the Lean proof on an example and extracting its intermediate state. A user study (n = 16) shows potential advantages of this approach: in a proof-understanding task, participants who used the explorability features wrote proof descriptions that an instructor preferred over those written with a proof-and-chatbot baseline, and gave more correct and more detailed answers to proof comprehension questions.

item.title: Narrative Keyframing for Generative Creative Writing
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
We introduce narrative keyframing, an interaction technique for AI-assisted creative writing that lets writers specify different types of narrative constraints at selected moments in a story, then use AI to generate intervening prose. Inspired by the use of keyframing in animation, narrative keyframing offers a flexible way to connect story planning with adaptive control over generated text. We explore three types of keyframes: plot keyframes define significant events in a story, character keyframes represent how individual characters change over the narrative, and perspective keyframes capture how individual characters experience different events through first-person narratives. Plot and character keyframes offer a flexible way to adapt the type of high-level conditioning explored in previous AI writing tools to more customizable, iterative, and fine-scale control, while perspective keyframes add a new way to control characterization and focalization by using first-person narratives as an intermediary. Through a user study, we show that narrative keyframing supports a more controllable, transparent, and engaging way to use generative AI in creative writing.

item.title: FabDreamer: Exploring the Image-to-Physical Workflow Through AI-Assisted Layered Fabrication
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Generative AI lets anyone create rich visual content in seconds, yet translating that content into a physically fabricable artifact still demands manual decomposition, occlusion repair, and structural verification that most tools leave entirely to the user. We present FabDreamer, an image-to-physical system that carries an image to fabrication-ready SVGs through three stages with deliberately staged AI initiative: (1) AI leads decomposition into depth-ordered layers, (2) assists on demand during creative editing with real-time 3D preview, and (3) advises on structural integrity before export. We instantiate this workflow for layered laser-cut art and evaluate it through three rounds including a formative analysis, an early prototype user evaluation (N=13), and a cross-domain practitioner study with specialists from 6 fabrication domains (N=6). Our findings show that physical awareness during design opens creative opportunities beyond error prevention, that practitioners appropriate the system’s generic geometric operations for their own domains, and that the fabrication agent covers geometry-readable constraints while domain knowledge remains with the maker.

item.title: Interactively Teaching Collaborative Physical Tasks to Generative AI with Narrated Demonstrations
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Enabling users to teach computers how to perform physical tasks is a long-standing goal in HCI. Prior work has explored learning from demonstration, but demonstrations often underspecify intent. Advances in generative AI enable a combination of demonstration and verbal narration to disambiguate intent. However, it remains largely unexplored how to design interfaces that leverage such narrated demonstrations to teach collaborative physical tasks. To probe this design space, we present a prototype system, Apprento, that models physical tasks as programs via generative AI with three integrated interfaces: (1) a teaching interface for providing narrated demonstrations in mixed reality, (2) an inspection interface for visualizing generated programs as decision-flow diagrams and program executions, and (3) a correction interface for iteratively refining generated programs. Across these interfaces, narrated demonstrations serve as a communication modality between users and the system. In a study with 20 participants teaching soccer skills, we identify differing user expectations around authoring and teaching collaborative tasks, as well as key design tensions between task complexity and program interpretability, and between program expressivity and accuracy. We discuss implications for designing future systems that support symbolic modeling of collaborative physical tasks through narrated demonstrations.

item.title: Who's Keeping Score? Interactive Steering of LLM-Powered Scoring with Attune
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to score text records at scale (e.g., rating candidate resumes on a 1–5 scale). However, existing LLM-powered approaches do not account for the fact that effective scoring requires both holistic understanding of records and locally consistent judgments across similar ones. We present Attune, a mixed-initiative system for steerable LLM-powered scoring. Given a task description and scoring range, Attune performs pairwise comparisons across records to develop a global understanding first, and then resolves these comparisons into consistent score assignments—deriving scoring criteria and rules bottom-up in the process. These serve as shared representations of scoring logic that users can inspect and edit. Based on insights from a formative study (n = 12), Attune’s interface introduces novel steering interactions that allow users to deterministically refine scoring logic. Users can provide examples, directly edit criteria, rules, or target distributions, and give natural language feedback—with all refinements compiling into constraints that guide re-scoring. We validate our approach through a technical evaluation across three workloads and a user study with domain experts (n = 8) in healthcare, law, education, and AI evaluation.

item.title: VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Great fiction earns its verisimilitude through precise details, from how a longsword is gripped to pierce armor gaps to why a bleeding corpse cannot yet smell of decay, weaving domain expertise into the fabric of invented worlds. Current AI writing tools offer limited support for discovering and integrating unfamiliar domain knowledge into narrative. They require explicit queries that authors cannot formulate, generate finished prose that risks homogenizing voice, or assist only within the boundaries of what authors already know. We argue that AI should reveal latent knowledge gaps to writers while preserving their agency to transform discovered knowledge into authentic prose. Grounded in formative interviews with 9 fiction writers, we present VeriForge, a mixed-initiative writing system that divides cognitive labor so that the system assumes initiative over domain discovery while the author retains full initiative over narrative synthesis. VeriForge realizes this through three complementary mechanisms. Proactive inline highlighting flags potential knowledge gaps as authors draft. Dual-stream querying pairs conversational responses with source-anchored Knowledge Cards for direct fact extraction. A spatial Knowledge Canvas allows authors to organize and connect discovered knowledge across their writing. These mechanisms are powered by a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation pipeline grounded in domain-specific source materials. A within-subjects user study (N=12) provides preliminary evidence that this paradigm helps authors recognize previously overlooked knowledge gaps, supports creative exploration, and is perceived by expert raters to produce passages with stronger domain grounding in a controlled cold-start writing task.

item.title: DocuDebug: A Graph-Supported Interactive Editor for Verifying and Maintaining Internal Logical Consistency
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
While large language models (LLMs) accelerate report generation, maintaining logical consistency during revisions increases the cognitive load, and delegating this task to LLMs often results in unpredictable global overwrites. To address this, we present DocuDebug, an interactive editor that reframes document verification as a software engineering task. The system models a document’s logical structure and citations as an explicit dependency graph. Through a linter-like interface, users receive real-time warnings for logical conflicts and propagate localized edits with guided precision. In a within-subjects study with 12 professional writers, DocuDebug guided precise, necessary corrections, improving precision over threefold and reducing over-editing from over 40% to under 5%. Furthermore, objective logs revealed that users avoided blind acceptance, actively deliberating over each warning for nearly three minutes. This work demonstrates how structured visual diagnostics can shift AI-assisted writing from opaque global generation to systematic, user-controlled co-creation.

item.title: InvisiSpeech: Making Silent Speech Invisible through a Miniature Intraoral Sensor
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Silent speech promises private interaction, but existing implementations often rely on visible sensors or conspicuous articulation, which limits their discretion in everyday use. We present InvisiSpeech, an intraoral interface that remains hidden from outside view and supports silent speech input with minimal lip movement and without drawing visual attention. Our custom flex-PCB device is housed in a biocompatible SLA-printed dental brace and attaches around the back molar. This mount couples a voice-pickup sensor to the tooth for input sensing, which our embedded microcontroller transfers via Bluetooth. Our evaluation with 15 participants shows that InvisiSpeech achieves up to 91.5% recognition accuracy on 50 sentence-level commands and maintains robustness in noisy environments. Participants also reported high wearability and perceived social acceptance, highlighting the practicality of our approach for daily use. We demonstrate three applications of our system: hands-free human–AI interaction in public, discreet interaction in a quiet public place, and subtle communication in a privacy-sensitive context. Our results establish invisible silent speech as a practical interaction paradigm for real-world use outside controlled settings.

item.title: Mirror Skin: In Situ Visualization of Robot Touch Intent on Robot Skin
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Effective communication of robot touch intent is essential for safe and predictable physical human-robot interaction. While intent communication has been widely studied, existing approaches lack the spatial specificity and semantic depth necessary to efficiently convey robot touch intent. We present Mirror Skin, a cephalopod-inspired concept that mirrors in-situ visual representations of a human’s body parts onto the corresponding robot’s touch region to communicate who shall initiate touch, where it will occur, and when it is imminent. We informed the design of Mirror Skin through a structured design exploration with experts and demonstrate the real-world feasibility of Mirror Skin with a proof-of-concept prototype. User studies in VR and with the physical prototype showed that Mirror Skin significantly improves accuracy and response times for interpreting touch intent and improves the user experience during physical human-robot interactions.

item.title: Micro-Edits: Computational Support for Fine-Scale Edits in Film
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
In film editing, every frame matters. While macro, content-level edits shape the high-level narrative of a film, small local edits often control timing and direct visual attention. For example, editors can adjust the precise timing of clips to control the length of a meaningful silence, or cut to shots that highlight a specific character’s reactions to important moments. These small, detailed edits are slow and tedious to make in standard editing tools because users have to map high-level narrative goals to low-level frame-by-frame adjustments. At the same time, these fine-scale adjustments, which we call micro-edits, can be nuanced and expressive, with different choices serving different creative goals. In this work, we start by conducting a formative study with professional editors to understand the structure of micro-edits and how they are used. We then derive a mathematical formalization for this structure to develop tools that leverage AI and optimization to make exploring micro-edits simpler and more efficient for users. Finally, we validate our tools in multiple user studies and a wide range of video examples.

item.title: MAIC-UI: Making Interactive Courseware with Generative UI
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Creating interactive STEM courseware traditionally requires HTML/CSS/JavaScript expertise, leaving barriers for educators. While generative AI can produce HTML codes, existing tools generate static presentations rather than interactive simulations, struggle with long documents, and lack pedagogical accuracy mechanisms. Furthermore, full regeneration for modifications requires 200–600 seconds, disrupting creative flow. We present MAIC-UI, a zero-code authoring system that enables educators to create and rapidly edit interactive courseware from textbooks, PPTs, and PDFs. MAIC-UI employs: (1) structured knowledge analysis with multi-modal understanding to ensure pedagogical rigor; (2) a two-stage generate-verify-optimize pipeline separating content alignment from visual refinement; and (3) Click-to-Locate editing with Unified Diff-based incremental generation achieving sub-10-second iteration cycles. A controlled lab study with 40 participants shows MAIC-UI reduces editing iterations (4.9 vs. 7.0) and significantly improves learnability and controllability compared to direct Text-to-HTML generation. A three-month classroom deployment with 53 high school students demonstrates that MAIC-UI fosters learning agency and reduces outcome disparities—the pilot class achieved 9.21-point gains in STEM subjects compared to -2.32 points in control classes. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-MAIC/MAIC-UI.

item.title: Map2Video: Guiding Real-World-Grounded AI Video Generation
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
AI video generation lowers barriers to video creation, but existing tools provide limited support for grounding content in real-world locations, restricting their use in applications such as film previsualization and scenario generation. In practice, users rely on verbose textual descriptions or reference images using on-site photos or street view imagery (SVI), which are cumbersome and unreliable across shots. Our formative study with five filmmakers revealed challenges in shot composition, character motion, and camera control when using SVI with an image-to-video tool. We present Map2Video, a system for guiding SVI-grounded AI video generation through map-based character trajectory annotation and direct manipulation of cameras and character masks defined in geodetic coordinates and projected onto panoramic screen coordinates. In an evaluation with twelve filmmakers, Map2Video provided stronger controllability for both scene replication and open-ended creative exploration, reduced cognitive effort, and improved spatial consistency across multiple shots compared to an image-to-video baseline.

item.title: MultiVerse: A Creator-Centered Approach to Steering Context-Adaptive Lyrics
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Generative AI may enable new forms of context-aware creative expression by dynamically tailoring media content to its consumption context. For instance, AI systems could adapt song lyrics to the listener and their current activity. However, existing media adaptation systems primarily optimize for audience experience, often neglecting artists’ intent, style, and preference. We address this challenge by introducing a novel creator-centered approach to adaptive media authoring and present MultiVerse, a system that instantiates this approach for steering adaptive lyrics. Our approach allows creators to explicitly author controls based on their intent, lyric structure, and audience context, and uses rule-based validations to ensure controls are followed. We conducted a study with 10 songwriters, comparing MultiVerse with a prompting-based workflow for composing adaptive lyrics. The comparison revealed that creators preferred to author how lyrics adapt by explicitly specifying relevant context and adaptation constraints, while recognizing trade-offs in flexibility and iteration speed. Interviews further revealed that creators viewed adaptive media as enabling new forms of audience connection, introducing a distinct creative process, favoring new compositional strategies, and reshaping notions of authorship.

item.title: CinemaWorld: Generative Augmented Reality with LLMs and 3D Scene Generation for Movie Augmentation
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
We introduce CinemaWorld, a generative augmented reality system that augments the viewer’s physical surroundings with automatically generated mixed reality 3D content extracted from and synchronized with 2D movie scenes. Our system preprocesses films to extract key features using multimodal large language models (LLMs), generates dynamic 3D augmentations with generative AI, and embeds them spatially into the viewer’s physical environment on the Meta Quest 3. To identify key augmentation techniques for CinemaWorld, we conducted an elicitation study with eight film students, which led us to identify several key augmentation types, including particle effects, surrounding objects, textural overlays, character-driven augmentation, and lighting effects. We evaluated our system through a technical evaluation (N=100 video clips), a user evaluation (comparison study: N=12 and in-the-wild study: N=8), and expert interviews with film creators (N=8). Results indicate that CinemaWorld enhances immersion and enjoyment, suggesting its potential to enrich the film-viewing experience.

item.title: TailorCoPilot: Enabling Agentic Pattern Making with Version-Controlled State Tracking
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Experience-driven manufacturing, such as garment pattern making, faces a severe generational skills gap because its core expertise relies on undocumented tacit knowledge forged through day-to-day practice. To address this challenge, we present TailorCoPilot, an agentic pattern-making system built upon a specially designed version-control backend TailorTrace. TailorTrace models sewing patterns as structured, discrete states and records their transformations during the pattern-making process as explicit operation sequences defined upon the geometry primitives in the sewing pattern (panels, edges, vertices and stitches). Integrated into a conventional pattern-making GUI, TailorTrace enables seamless documentation of senior experts’ tacit pattern-making knowledge without breaking their daily workflow. The documented knowledge further offers interactive, pedagogical scaffolding for novices, while providing a robust foundation to power TailorCoPilot and train future generative AI models. In a user study with novices and advanced novices, TailorCoPilot improved task completion rates, reduced time and perceived workload, and yielded higher-quality artifacts compared to skill-appropriate baselines. Ultimately, TailorCoPilot demonstrates a viable pathway to capture practice-based expertise, operationalizing it to support both generative AI advancements and human apprenticeship.

item.title: PATHWiSE: Empowering Teachers with a Generative AI Authoring System for Personalized Robot-Assisted Learning
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Homework assignments often lack the personalized guidance and social interaction crucial for learning. Social robots offer a promising way to bring personalization and interactive support into learning activities; however, teachers rarely have the technical expertise needed to operate robots, let alone create or customize robot-assisted learning (RAL) lessons. To address this challenge, we introduce PATHWiSE, a robust, no-code authoring system designed to empower teachers to create custom RAL activities. Developed through participatory co-design activities with middle school science teachers and students and iteratively refined through multiple user studies, PATHWiSE enables educators to author, preview, and personalize RAL activities that can be tailored to different robot platforms and delivered with either in-person or on-screen robots. The system maintains a flexible trigger-action programming model to define robot expressions contextually related to lesson materials. Through integrated teacher- and student-facing portals, teachers can deploy RAL lessons using a lightweight and portable browser-based approach that affords integration with a wide range of systems. AI-assisted comment and emotion-expression generation tools augment teacher lesson creation while preserving teacher autonomy and expertise in content design. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of PATHWiSE, including its authoring workflow, interface architecture, backend integration, and representative use cases drawn from iterative studies to illustrate the capabilities of the full system.

item.title: PartInteractor: Intent-Driven Part-Aware 3D Authoring for Continuous Co-Creation in XR
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
As Extended Reality (XR) evolves into an immersive computing medium, interactive 3D authoring becomes essential for creative and functional workflows. However, existing generative XR systems produce monolithic outputs lacking explicit semantic structure, limiting post-generation control. We introduce PartInteractor, a representation-to-interaction framework that investigates how semantic part hierarchies can be incorporated into generative XR authoring, and exposed as first-class, directly manipulable units, turning one-shot prompt-to-object generation into continuous component-level co-creation. PartInteractor supports speech, sketch, and image inputs, integrating an LLM interpreter with a retrieval-generation strategy to scaffold user intent prior to 3D generation. Instead of producing monolithic objects, our system generates semantically decomposed 3D assets with explicit part hierarchies, enabling rich component-level interaction over object structure and composition. Our evaluations suggest that part-aware representation increases post-generation control and reduces reliance on whole-object regeneration, while intent scaffolding mitigates ambiguity and improves intent-result alignment, together supporting more expressive and controllable human-AI co-creation workflows. These results highlight part-aware representation and intent scaffolding as promising design considerations for future generative XR authoring systems.

item.title: As effective as the teacher, but less motivating: a randomized controlled comparison of AI-generated and teacher feedback on students’ writing performance and intrinsic motivation
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers scalable feedback on student writing; however, its effects on writing performance and motivation relative to teacher feedback remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on Feedback Intervention Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this study examined the comparative effectiveness of AI-generated and teacher-provided feedback on students’ writing performance and motivational outcomes. Methods A randomized controlled study assigned 312 undergraduate students to one of three conditions: AI-generated feedback, teacher feedback, or a control condition without substantive feedback. A total of 287 participants were included in the analyses. The study evaluated revised-essay quality, feedback engagement, writing self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, perceived relatedness to the feedback source, and AI literacy. Results Both AI-generated feedback and teacher feedback produced higher revised-essay quality than the control condition, with effect sizes of d = 0.60 and d = 0.59, respectively. The two feedback conditions were statistically equivalent within a prespecified equivalence margin of ±0.35 standard deviations. Feedback engagement, but not writing self-efficacy, statistically accounted for the observed performance advantage. Teacher feedback elicited higher intrinsic motivation than AI-generated feedback, although AI-generated feedback also yielded higher intrinsic motivation than the control condition. This motivational difference was associated with perceived relatedness to the feedback source. The indirect effects identified in the analyses are associational rather than causal. AI literacy did not significantly moderate the effect of feedback on writing performance ( p = 0.058). Discussion Within the context of a single feedback-and-revision cycle at one institution, the findings suggest that AI-generated feedback can achieve writing-performance outcomes comparable to those of teacher feedback, while providing weaker motivational support. These results highlight the potential value of blended feedback approaches that combine the scalability of AI-generated feedback with the relational and motivational strengths of teacher–student interaction. Further research across multiple institutions and repeated feedback cycles is needed to establish the generalizability and longer-term implications of these findings.

item.title: Making argumentative work visible in GenAI-mediated assessment: an exploratory LLM simulation and questionnaire study in university ideological and political education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative AI weakens the correspondence between the final text of an assignment and the argumentative work involved in producing it. This study examined how task structure and AI-use instructions shape evidence use, engagement with objections, and revision in university ideological and political education. Methods An LLM simulation crossed three task formats—position essays, evidence-integration memoranda, and follow-up-and-revision defense tasks—with three AI-use scenarios—simulated no-AI, responsible collaboration, and concealed ghostwriting. Two raters coded 148 generated texts with the Textual Response Artifact Scoring Index (TRASI), and an anonymous questionnaire collected 268 evaluations of 27 selected texts. Results Responsible collaboration produced the highest overall rubric score ( M = 3.32). Evidence-integration memoranda ( M = 3.16) and follow-up-and-revision defenses ( M = 3.10) exceeded position essays ( M = 2.63). Position essays varied most across the three AI-use scenarios, whereas the memorandum and defense showed narrower differences because their instructions already required source explanation or response and revision. Questionnaire participants distinguished the same task functions: memoranda were rated highest for source–claim linkage, and defenses for counterargument response and revision explanation. Open-ended responses associated evidence integration, comparison of reasons, and revision with thinking, while formulaic structure, over-polished expression, and generic abstraction were associated with AI-like writing. Discussion Task structure and AI-use instructions were functionally complementary. Structured tasks elicited source explanation or challenge and revision directly, so responsible collaboration added its largest contribution in the general position essay. GenAI-mediated assessment can therefore be designed around the argumentative decisions that writers are required to document.

item.title: Process visualization feedback in news translation: a controlled intervention study of human-AI interaction using multimodal process data
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction This study examines process visualization feedback in news translation. Methods Framed within Krings' three-dimensional model, a pretest-posttest control group design was employed with 24 MTI students. The final analytic sample comprised 22 participants (11 experimental, 11 control). The experimental group ( n = 11) received personalized process visualizations and structured reflection; the control group ( n = 11) received conventional product-oriented feedback. Translation scores were available for both groups at T1 and T2, and complete process data (Inputlog, screen recording) were available for the experimental group at both time points. Results Within the experimental group, within-subject comparisons showed changes in all three dimensions: in the temporal dimension, increased pause time proportion indicated heightened metacognitive engagement ( p = 0.011); in the technical dimension, the meaning-level revision ratio increased significantly from 18.1% to 28.4% ( p = 0.002), indicating a shift from surface-level correction to deeper substantive refinement; in the cognitive dimension, participants made more strategic use of external sources, with significant increases in search engine queries ( p = 0.02) and knowledge-based searches ( p = 0.01). Rich-points analysis of problem-triggered pauses revealed a shift from linguistic toward textual and extralinguistic problems ( p = 0.038, p = 0.015). A mixed-design ANOVA revealed a significant Group × Time interaction ( p = 0.038, η p 2 = 0.198). Thematic analysis of reflective journals ( n = 22) and interviews ( n = 6) revealed two overarching themes: metacognitive awareness (54 references) of inefficient process patterns and competency gaps, and strategic regulation (60 references) in external source use and text-level restructuring. Discussion These findings suggest that process visualization feedback was associated with enhanced metacognitive awareness and strategic regulation, and may support learners in becoming more reflective, strategic, and autonomous in human-AI collaborative news translation.

item.title: Add-on efficacy of neurofeedback-augmented mindfulness training for stress reduction: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Stress is a psychophysiological response that occurs when environmental demands exceed an individual’s coping capacity, and it is closely linked to many psychosomatic disorders. Mindfulness training can effectively reduce stress, but conventional mindfulness training (CM) places high demands on self-monitoring ability, which limits its effect. Neurofeedback-augmented mindfulness training (NM) provides real-time feedback on brain activity signals and may help address this limitation. However, most existing studies are small-sample RCTs, and their conclusions remain inconsistent. This study used a systematic review and meta-analysis to compare the overall effects of NM and CM on stress reduction and related mental health outcomes, aiming to provide evidence-based guidance for intervention selection in non-clinical young and middle-aged populations with mental health needs. We searched MEDLINE, PubMed, Scopus, CNKI, the Cochrane Library, and the ClinicalTrials registry databases. Publication dates were limited to January 2016 to August 2026. Five randomized controlled trials with 358 participants in total were included, and outcomes included stress, anxiety, depression, sleep quality, phone addiction, no-phone phobia, fatigue, neuroticism, and psychological resilience. Extracted data were pooled using a random-effects model, and sensitivity analyses were performed based on heterogeneity. In terms of stress improvement, NM showed a trend toward superiority over CM (SMD 0.65, P = 0.0009), with robust conclusions. For anxiety, two studies comparing NM with CM consistently supported the superiority of NM (SMD 0.67–0.87, both P < 0.01); however, evidence comparing NM with mental health education was inconsistent. For depression, NM showed a trend toward superiority over mental health education (SMD 0.41, P = 0.04), though the robustness was limited; evidence comparing NM with CM was limited and inconsistent. For sleep quality, no advantage of NM was observed compared with either CM or mental health education (SMD 0.05, P = 0.74), and this negative conclusion was robust. For the remaining outcomes, evidence was insufficient or inconsistent, and no definitive conclusions could be drawn. The preliminary evidence from this study suggests that, among non-clinical young and middle-aged adults, NM demonstrated relatively consistent potential advantages in improving stress, with robust directional findings. For anxiety, NM may offer benefits over CM, although the certainty of evidence is limited; evidence comparing NM with mental health education remains inconsistent. For depression, NM may be superior to mental health education, but the robustness is insufficient, and evidence comparing NM with CM is limited and inconsistent. For sleep quality, no advantage of NM was observed, and this negative finding was robust. For the remaining outcomes, definitive conclusions could not be drawn due to the very small number of studies or inconsistent results. These findings are limited by the small number of included studies, the fact that some outcomes were derived from single studies, and the exclusively non-clinical nature of the samples. Further high-quality randomized controlled trials are warranted to verify these results.

item.title: Leader-Follower Hierarchical Role Effects on Individual and Shared Trust in Mixed Human-AI Teams
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Human-AI Teams (HATs) are evolving into increasingly complex multi-human multi-agent structures, including those with hierarchical leadership and role accountability. Conventionally, humans have primarily taken leadership positions, directing and supervising autonomous agents. However, emerging HAT contexts now enable humans to assume a wider range of hierarchical roles within teams, including both leader and follower positions. Despite these developments, empirical research on non-dyadic HATs remains limited, leaving important questions regarding trust and teamwork in complex team structures largely unexplored. In this study, we investigate how hierarchical roles differentially shape trust in AI teammates and trust in the team as a whole, as well as how role-based trust divergence associates with overall team outcomes. We find that trust varies significantly by the trustor’s role, yet shared trust and reduced trust divergence across teammates are critical for better team performance. Accordingly, it is important to support shared team cognition and mitigate trust divergence.

item.title: From Narrative to Intent Schema Architecture: An Artificial Intelligence System for Human-Centered Advising Decision Support
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Transfer advising is a high-uncertainty setting where students rarely ask well-structured questions and advisors must infer intent from fragmented narratives across conflicting institutional policies. This research presents a human-centered AI framework that transforms naturalistic student discourse into structured advising intents, supporting a student-facing advising assistant whose explainable outputs are designed to support advisor review. Using 19,668 transfer-related Reddit posts, it surfaces recurring advising intents via extraction, clustering, and structured labeling, then routes student questions to them. On a proof-of-concept benchmark it reached 90% intent-level and 86% question-level accuracy, turning advising knowledge into transparent structures that support scalable, human-centered advising.
